plan.topic_summary: Base editing is a gene-editing approach enabling precise single-nucleotide modifications without double-strand breaks, and its progression from bench to clinic over the next 1–5 years will determine whether it becomes a dominant modality in the gene-editing tool market or remains a niche complement to other editing strategies.

sources.title: Base Editing and Prime Editing
sources.abstract: Abstract The development of new adaptations of CRISPR-based genome editing platforms, such as base editing and prime editing, made it possible to broaden the scope and applications of genome editing in plants. First base editing and, more recently, prime editing evade the creation of double-stranded breaks in deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and the requirement of donor template of DNA for repair while enhancing editing efficiency and product purity over CRISPR/Cas9. As base-pair changes in genomic DNA determine many significant agronomic traits, crop varieties can be developed by precisely converting specific single bases in plant genomes. While base editing can introduce specific nucleotide changes, such as transition and transversion mutations in the targeted region, prime editing can create precise insertions, deletions, and all 12 types of point mutations using the “search-and-replace” method. This chapter provides the basic principles of base editing and prime editing technologies and their practical applications in plants. The chapter also summarizes the recent breakthroughs in applying base and prime editors in diverse plant species, including their use in improving disease resistance, herbicide resistance, nutritional quality, crop yield, and quality. Finally, this chapter aims to clearly understand base editing and prime editing in plants by outlining potential developments.

sources.title: STACKFEED: Structured Textual Actor-Critic Knowledge Base Editing with FeedBack
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: Industry Track 2588-2606
sources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate incorrect or outdated information, especially in low-resource settings or when dealing with private data. To address this, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) uses external knowledge bases (KBs), but these can also suffer from inaccuracies. We introduce STACKFEED, a novel Structured Textual Actor-Critic Knowledge base editing with FEEDback approach that iteratively refines the KB based on expert feedback using a multi-actor, centralized critic reinforcement learning framework. STACKFEED defines a ReACT actor agent on each document to perform structured edits based on document specific targeted instructions. Experimental results showcase that STACKFEED significantly improves KB quality and performance of the RAG system. We evaluate STACKFEED on low-resource programming problems, modified python packaged and factual question-answering tasks.

sources.title: Base editing rescue of spinal muscular atrophy in cells and in mice
sources.abstract: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), the leading genetic cause of infant mortality, arises from survival motor neuron (SMN) protein insufficiency resulting from SMN1 loss. Approved therapies circumvent endogenous SMN regulation and require repeated dosing or may wane. We describe genome editing of SMN2 , an insufficient copy of SMN1 harboring a C6>T mutation, to permanently restore SMN protein levels and rescue SMA phenotypes. We used nucleases or base editors to modify five SMN2 regulatory regions. Base editing converted SMN2 T6>C, restoring SMN protein levels to wild type. Adeno-associated virus serotype 9–mediated base editor delivery in Δ7SMA mice yielded 87% average T6>C conversion, improved motor function, and extended average life span, which was enhanced by one-time base editor and nusinersen coadministration (111 versus 17 days untreated). These findings demonstrate the potential of a one-time base editing treatment for SMA.

sources.title: DreamOmni3: Scribble-based Editing and Generation
sources.abstract: Recently unified generation and editing models have achieved remarkable success with their impressive performance. These models rely mainly on text prompts for instruction-based editing and generation, but language often fails to capture users intended edit locations and fine-grained visual details. To this end, we propose two tasks: scribble-based editing and generation, that enables more flexible creation on graphical user interface (GUI) combining user textual, images, and freehand sketches. We introduce DreamOmni3, tackling two challenges: data creation and framework design. Our data synthesis pipeline includes two parts: scribble-based editing and generation. For scribble-based editing, we define four tasks: scribble and instruction-based editing, scribble and multimodal instruction-based editing, image fusion, and doodle editing. Based on DreamOmni2 dataset, we extract editable regions and overlay hand-drawn boxes, circles, doodles or cropped image to construct training data. For scribble-based generation, we define three tasks: scribble and instruction-based generation, scribble and multimodal instruction-based generation, and doodle generation, following similar data creation pipelines. For the framework, instead of using binary masks, which struggle with complex edits involving multiple scribbles, images, and instructions, we propose a joint input scheme that feeds both the original and scribbled source images into the model, using different colors to distinguish regions and simplify processing. By applying the same index and position encodings to both images, the model can precisely localize scribbled regions while maintaining accurate editing. Finally, we establish comprehensive benchmarks for these tasks to promote further research. Experimental results demonstrate that DreamOmni3 achieves outstanding performance, and models and code will be publicly released.

sources.title: Base editing correction of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in human cardiomyocytes and humanized mice
DreamOmni2: Multimodal Instruction-based Editing and Generation
sources.abstract: Recent advancements in instruction-based image editing and subject-driven generation have garnered significant attention, yet both tasks still face limitations in meeting practical user needs. Instruction-based editing relies solely on language instructions, which often fail to capture specific editing details, making reference images necessary. Meanwhile, subject-driven generation is limited to combining concrete objects or people, overlooking broader, abstract concepts. To address these challenges, we propose two novel tasks: multimodal instruction-based editing and generation. These tasks support both text and image instructions and extend the scope to include both concrete and abstract concepts, greatly enhancing their practical applications. We introduce DreamOmni2, tackling two primary challenges: data creation and model framework design. Our data synthesis pipeline consists of three steps: (1) using a feature mixing method to create extraction data for both abstract and concrete concepts, (2) generating multimodal instruction-based editing training data using the editing and extraction models, and (3) further applying the extraction model to create training data for multimodal instruction-based editing. For the framework, to handle multi-image input, we propose an index encoding and position encoding shift scheme, which helps the model distinguish images and avoid pixel confusion. Additionally, we introduce joint training with the VLM and our generation/editing model to better process complex instructions. In addition, we have proposed comprehensive benchmarks for these two new tasks to drive their development. Experiments show that DreamOmni2 has achieved impressive results. Models and codes will be released.

sources.title: Base-Edited CAR7 T Cells for Relapsed T-Cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
sources.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cytidine deamination that is guided by clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) can mediate a highly precise conversion of one nucleotide into another - specifically, cytosine to thymine - without generating breaks in DNA. Thus, genes can be base-edited and rendered inactive without inducing translocations and other chromosomal aberrations. The use of this technique in patients with relapsed childhood T-cell leukemia is being investigated. METHODS: We used base editing to generate universal, off-the-shelf chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. Healthy volunteer donor T cells were transduced with the use of a lentivirus to express a CAR with specificity for CD7 (CAR7), a protein that is expressed in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). We then used base editing to inactivate three genes encoding CD52 and CD7 receptors and the β chain of the αβ T-cell receptor to evade lymphodepleting serotherapy, CAR7 T-cell fratricide, and graft-versus-host disease, respectively. We investigated the safety of these edited cells in three children with relapsed leukemia. RESULTS: The first patient, a 13-year-old girl who had relapsed T-cell ALL after allogeneic stem-cell transplantation, had molecular remission within 28 days after infusion of a single dose of base-edited CAR7 (BE-CAR7). She then received a reduced-intensity (nonmyeloablative) allogeneic stem-cell transplant from her original donor, with successful immunologic reconstitution and ongoing leukemic remission. BE-CAR7 cells from the same bank showed potent activity in two other patients, and although fatal fungal complications developed in one patient, the other patient underwent allogeneic stem-cell transplantation while in remission. Serious adverse events included cytokine release syndrome, multilineage cytopenia, and opportunistic infections. CONCLUSIONS: The interim results of this phase 1 study support further investigation of base-edited T cells for patients with relapsed leukemia and indicate the anticipated risks of immunotherapy-related complications. (Funded by the Medical Research Council and others; ISRCTN number, ISRCTN15323014.).

sources.title: DiffVax: Optimization-Free Image Immunization Against Diffusion-Based Editing
sources.abstract: Current image immunization defense techniques against diffusion-based editing embed imperceptible noise into target images to disrupt editing models. However, these methods face scalability challenges, as they require time-consuming optimization for each image separately, taking hours for small batches. To address these challenges, we introduce DiffVax, a scalable, lightweight, and optimization-free framework for image immunization, specifically designed to prevent diffusion-based editing. Our approach enables effective generalization to unseen content, reducing computational costs and cutting immunization time from days to milliseconds, achieving a speedup of 250,000x. This is achieved through a loss term that ensures the failure of editing attempts and the imperceptibility of the perturbations. Extensive qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate that our model is scalable, optimization-free, adaptable to various diffusion-based editing tools, robust against counter-attacks, and, for the first time, effectively protects video content from editing. More details are available in https://diffvax.github.io/ .

MedREK: Retrieval-Based Editing for Medical LLMs with Key-Aware Prompts
sources.abstract: LLMs hold great promise for healthcare applications, but the rapid evolution of medical knowledge and errors in training data often cause them to generate outdated or inaccurate information, limiting their applicability in high-stakes clinical practice. Model editing has emerged as a potential remedy without full retraining. While parameter-based editing often compromises locality and is thus ill-suited for the medical domain, retrieval-based editing offers a more viable alternative. However, it still faces two critical challenges: (1) representation overlap within the medical knowledge space often causes inaccurate retrieval and reduces editing accuracy; (2) existing methods are restricted to single-sample edits, while batch-editing remains largely unexplored despite its importance for real-world medical applications. To address these challenges, we first construct MedVersa, an enhanced benchmark with broader coverage of medical subjects, designed to evaluate both single and batch edits under strict locality constraints. We then propose MedREK, a retrieval-based editing framework that integrates a shared query-key module for precise matching with an attention-based prompt encoder for informative guidance. Experimental results on various medical benchmarks demonstrate that our MedREK achieves superior performance across different core metrics and provides the first validated solution for batch-editing in medical LLMs. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/mylittleriver/MedREK.

sources.title: What Is "Base Editing"? Understanding BASE EDITING: A Targeted Evolution of CRISPR Technology
sources.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sources.abstract: What Is “Base Editing”? Understanding BASE EDITING: A Targeted Evolution of CRISPR Technology Authored by Dr. H.K. Saboowala, this book explores "base editing"—a breakthrough advancement in genetic engineering that represents the next evolution of CRISPR technology. Traditional CRISPR methods rely on cutting through both strands of DNA, which can introduce unpredictable errors during cellular repair. In contrast, base editing acts as a highly precise "molecular pencil," directly rewriting single DNA letters without fracturing the genetic backbone. This comprehensive text demystifies how these tools operate, details the different types of base editors, highlights current clinical breakthroughs, and outlines the future of safer, highly targeted gene therapies for genetic diseases. Author website: https://drhakimemedivault.com Google Scholar Profile: https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=VnL3NuoAAAAJ&hl=en Google Books Catalog: https://books.google.com/books?q=inauthor:%22Hakim+Saboowala%22

sources.title: Taming Horizontal Instability in Merge Trees: On the Computation of a Comprehensive Deformation-based Edit Distance
sources.abstract: Comparative analysis of scalar fields in scientific visualization often involves distance functions on topological abstractions. This paper focuses on the merge tree abstraction (representing the nesting of sub- or superlevel sets) and proposes the application of the unconstrained deformation-based edit distance. Previous approaches on merge trees often suffer from instability: small perturbations in the data can lead to large distances of the abstractions. While some existing methods can handle so-called vertical instability, the unconstrained deformation-based edit distance addresses both vertical and horizontal instabilities, also called saddle swaps. We establish the computational complexity as NP-complete, and provide an integer linear program formulation for computation. Experimental results on the TOSCA shape matching ensemble provide evidence for the stability of the proposed distance. We thereby showcase the potential of handling saddle swaps for comparison of scalar fields through merge trees.

sources.title: Cytosine base editors induce off-target mutations and adverse phenotypic effects in transgenic mice
sources.abstract: Abstract Base editors have been reported to induce off-target mutations in cultured cells, mouse embryos and rice, but their long-term effects in vivo remain unknown. Here, we develop a Systematic evaluation Approach For gene Editing tools by Transgenic mIce (SAFETI), and evaluate the off-target effects of BE3, high fidelity version of CBE (YE1-BE3-FNLS) and ABE (ABE7.10F148A) in ~400 transgenic mice over 15 months. Whole-genome sequence analysis reveals BE3 expression generated de novo mutations in the offspring of transgenic mice. RNA-seq analysis reveals both BE3 and YE1-BE3-FNLS induce transcriptome-wide SNVs, and the numbers of RNA SNVs are positively correlated with CBE expression levels across various tissues. By contrast, ABE7.10F148A shows no detectable off-target DNA or RNA SNVs. Notably, we observe abnormal phenotypes including obesity and developmental delay in mice with permanent genomic BE3 overexpression during long-time monitoring, elucidating a potentially overlooked aspect of side effects of BE3 in vivo.

sources.title: Innovative Transformer Base Editor (tBE)-Mediated Editing at BCL11A Binding Motif Triggers High Level of γ-Globin Expression with No Observable Off-Target Mutations
sources.abstract: Activating the silent γ-globin expression is a universal therapeutic strategy for treating β-hemoglobinopathies including β-thalassemia and sickle cell disease. Several therapeutic target sites have been identified and the editing at these sites can reactivate γ-globin expression. In this study, we used a recently developed cytosine base editor, transformer base editor (tBE), which triggers no observable off-target mutations, to edit the therapeutic target sites for triggering γ-globin expression. Through editing six therapeutic sites, we found that the editing at BCL11A binding motif in the HBG1/2 promoters induced the highest γ-globin expression level. By comparing to other approaches such as Cas9 nuclease or other base editors, tBE-meditated editing at BCL11A binding motif induced higher fetal hemoglobin (HbF) expression and meanwhile did not trigger any detected DNA or RNA off-target mutations. Of note, tBE-mediated editing at the HBG1/2 promoters induced more robust HbF expression in the erythroid progeny from β 0/β 0 thalassemia patient-derived hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) than CRISPR/Cas9 approach. Moreover, persistent base editing by tBE was found in long-term repopulating hematopoietic stem cells. Taken together, this study demonstrates that tBE-mediated therapeutic base editing at BCL11A binding motif in HBG1/2 promoters is a safe and highly effective strategy for treating β-hemoglobinopathies.

sources.title: Split complementation of base editors to minimize off-target edits
Prediction of base editor off-targets by deep learning
sources.abstract: Due to the tolerance of mismatches between gRNA and targeting sequence, base editors frequently induce unwanted Cas9-dependent off-target mutations. Here, to develop models to predict such off-targets, we design gRNA-off- target pairs for adenine base editors (ABEs) and cytosine base editors (CBEs) and stably integrate them into the human cells. After five days of editing, we obtain valid efficiency datasets of 54,663 and 55,727 off-targets for ABEs and CBEs, respectively. We use the datasets to train deep learning models, resulting in ABEdeepoff and CBEdeepoff, which can predict off-target sites. We use these tools to predict off-targets for a panel of endogenous loci and achieve Spearman correlation values varying from 0.710 to 0.859. Finally, we develop an integrated tool that is freely accessible via an online web server http://www.deephf.com/#/bedeep/bedeepoff . These tools could facilitate minimizing the off-target effects of base editing.

Sensitive and unbiased genome-wide profiling of base-editor-induced off-target activity using CHANGE-seq-BE
sources.abstract: Detection of the off-target effects of base editors is important for identifying their safety risks but current methods for understanding their global activities have limitations in terms of sensitivity or bias by computationally selecting a subset of sites for experimental analysis. We present CHANGE-seq-BE, a method to assess the guide RNA-dependent off-target profile of both adenine and cytosine base editors that is simultaneously sensitive and unbiased. CHANGE-seq-BE relies on selective sequencing of base-editor-modified genomic DNA in vitro and provides comprehensive identification of genome-wide off-target mutations. We found that 98.8% of validated off-target sites were unique to ABE8e adenine base editors compared to Cas9 nuclease, suggesting substantially higher off-target activity of the former. We further applied CHANGE-seq-BE to support genotoxicity studies in an emergency investigational new drug application for customized adenine base editor treatment for a person with CD40L-deficient X-linked hyper IgM syndrome. Our results emphasize the importance of using a base-editor-specific method for identifying off-target activity.

sources.title: Base editing enables duplex point mutagenesis in Clostridium autoethanogenum at the price of numerous off-target mutations
sources.abstract: Base editors are recent multiplex gene editing tools derived from the Cas9 nuclease of Streptomyces pyogenes. They can target and modify a single nucleotide in the genome without inducing double-strand breaks (DSB) of the DNA helix. As such, they hold great potential for the engineering of microbes that lack effective DSB repair pathways such as homologous recombination (HR) or non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ). However, few applications of base editors have been reported in prokaryotes to date, and their advantages and drawbacks have not been systematically reported. Here, we used the base editors Target-AID and Target-AID-NG to introduce nonsense mutations into four different coding sequences of the industrially relevant Gram-positive bacterium Clostridium autoethanogenum. While up to two loci could be edited simultaneously using a variety of multiplexing strategies, most colonies exhibited mixed genotypes and most available protospacers led to undesired mutations within the targeted editing window. Additionally, fifteen off-target mutations were detected by sequencing the genome of the resulting strain, among them seven single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) in or near loci bearing some similarity with the targeted protospacers, one 15 nt duplication, and one 12 kb deletion which removed uracil DNA glycosylase (UDG), a key DNA repair enzyme thought to be an obstacle to base editing mutagenesis. A strategy to process prokaryotic single-guide RNA arrays by exploiting tRNA maturation mechanisms is also illustrated.

sources.title: Unbiased whole genome detection of ultrarare off‐target mutations in genome‐edited cell populations by HiFi sequencing
sources.abstract: Abstract DNA base editors (BEs) composed of a nuclease‐deficient Cas9 fused to a DNA‐modifying enzyme can achieve on‐target mutagenesis without creating double‐strand DNA breaks (DSBs). As a result, BEs generate far less DNA damage than traditional nuclease‐proficient Cas9 systems, which do rely on the creation of DSBs to achieve on‐target mutagenesis. The inability of BEs to create DSBs makes the detection of their undesired off‐target effects very difficult. PacBio HiFi sequencing can efficiently detect ultrarare mutations resulting from chemical mutagenesis in whole genomes with a sensitivity ~1 × 10−8 mutations per base pair. In this proof‐of‐principle study, we evaluated whether this technique could also detect the on‐ and off‐target mutations generated by a cytosine‐to‐thymine (C>T) BE targeting the LacZ gene in Escherichia coli (E. coli). HiFi sequencing detected on‐target mutant allele fractions ranging from ~7% to ~63%, depending on the single‐guide RNA (sgRNA) used, while no on‐target mutations were detected in controls lacking the BE. The presence of the BE resulted in a ~3‐fold increase in mutation frequencies compared to controls lacking the BE, irrespective of the sgRNA used. These increases were mostly composed of C:G>T:A substitutions distributed throughout the genome. Our results demonstrate that HiFi sequencing can efficiently identify on‐ and off‐target mutations in cell populations that have undergone genome editing.

sources.title: CRISPR Base-Editing for Correcting Monogenic Mutations: Optimization and Off-Target Profiling
sources.abstract: CRISPR base-editing has now emerged as a fast, accurate, and least disruptive technology to correct monogenic mutations in animal models, demonstrating direct A-G and C-T base conversions, without formation of two-stranded breaks. This review summarizes recent advances in optimization of base-editing systems, delivery, and optimization of off-target profiling of mice, zebrafish, rabbits, and livestock. The major results are reported on the development of better versions of the EsCs: BE4max, ABE8e, and high-fidelity Cas9 enzymes can be used to obtain better on-target specificity, whereas AAV vectors, LNPs, and mRNA-based delivery are important in enabling tissue-specific editing. Species-specific variability in off-target studies due to chromatin context and deaminase behavior raises the importance of standardized profiling pipelines. Although it has not been used in therapeutic contexts, despite considerable demonstrated capabilities in metabolic, ocular, and neuromuscular disease models, there are still challenges, including limitations in the use of PAM by bystanders, mosaicism, and long-term safety. All in all, this review provides basis on the possibility of further refinement of editors, safer methods of delivery, and ethical biosafety systems to develop CRISPR base-editing into effective preclinical and translational practices.

sources.title: High performance TadA-8e derived cytosine and dual base editors with undetectable off-target effects in plants
sources.abstract: Abstract Cytosine base editors (CBEs) and adenine base editors (ABEs) are powerful tools to install precise C-to-T and A-to-G base edits in living organisms. In recently years, a highly efficient ABE based on engineered TadA-8e, known as ABE8e, has been developed to confer highly efficient A-to-G editing in mammalian cells and plants. Interestingly, TadA-8e can be further evolved and engineered to confer cytosine base editing. In this study, we compare in rice and tomato cells a serial of engineered CBEs derived from TadA-8e and identify TadCBEa, TadCBEd, and TadCBEd_V106W as efficient CBEs with high editing purity, while maintaining the relatively narrow editing window of ABE8e. Excitingly, we show TadDE is a new class of dual base editor where a single deaminase domain promotes simultaneous C-to-T and A-to-G base editing in plant cells. Multiplexed base editing is demonstrated in transgenic rice plants with TadCBEa and TadDE. Furthermore, no off-target effects of TadCBEa and TadDE can be detected by whole genome and transcriptome sequencing of the transgenic lines, suggesting high editing specificity. Finally, we demonstrate two gain-of-function crop engineering applications in rice by using the efficient dual base editor, TadDE. In the first case, herbicide resistance alleles of OsALS are introduced by TadDE. In the second case, synonymous mutations are generated in OsSPL14 , making its transcript resistant to OsMIR156 -mediated degradation. Together, this study reports TadA-8e derived CBEs and a dual base editor with high editing activity, purity, and specificity. They are valuable additions to the expanding plant base editing toolbox.

findings.claim: Cytosine base editor (BE3) expression produced de novo mutations and adverse phenotypes (obesity, developmental delay) in a ~400-mouse, 15-month transgenic study. This is a long-term in vivo safety signal that short-term cell assays would not capture.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: One peer-reviewed study. The design uses permanent genomic overexpression, which is much higher and longer exposure than transient therapeutic delivery (LNP or mRNA). The finding therefore bounds the risk for constitutive expression and may overstate it for clinical use. The abstract reports no detectable off-target SNVs for ABE7.10F148A, so the risk appears editor-specific.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Whole-genome sequence analysis reveals BE3 expression generated de novo mutations in the offspring of transgenic mice.

findings.claim: A base-editor-specific genome-wide assay (CHANGE-seq-BE) found that nearly all validated off-target sites were unique to ABE8e compared with Cas9 nuclease. This suggests the highly active ABE8e has a distinct and possibly larger off-target footprint than nuclease editing, so DSB-free does not mean off-target-free.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The result comes from one abstract and an in vitro, guide-RNA-dependent method, which may not reflect cellular off-target frequency. It sits uneasily with the mouse finding that ABE7.10F148A showed no detectable off-target DNA or RNA SNVs (src_4f2097fc62). The editor variants, systems and assay sensitivities differ, so safety is likely variant- and method-dependent.
findings.supporting_excerpt: We found that 98.8% of validated off-target sites were unique to ABE8e adenine base editors compared to Cas9 nuclease, suggesting substantially higher off-target activity of the former.

findings.claim: Claims of 'no detectable' or 'undetectable' off-target effects depend on how sensitive and unbiased the detection method is. Absence of detected off-targets in several studies should not be read as absence of off-targets.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Several papers report no detectable off-targets: a conference abstract on tBE (src_d991e9043d), a title-only record on HBG promoter editing in HSCs (src_75ce59f10b), and a plant study using whole-genome and transcriptome sequencing (src_d9e3388c42). Against this, src_3e4582091d says the lack of DSBs makes base-editor off-target detection very difficult, and src_8f68bee9fc says existing methods are limited in sensitivity or biased by site selection. The tBE item is a conference abstract, so it is not full peer-reviewed evidence. The HBG paper has no abstract available here. The plant results concern rice and tomato, not human therapy. The detection ceilings of each study are not stated in the abstracts, so this is a gap in comparability, not proof of hidden off-targets.

findings.claim: Base editors can cause off-target RNA editing, not only DNA edits. RNA SNVs scaled with CBE expression level, and a 2025 paper titled as reporting RNA editing 'hotspots' suggests the issue is recurrent. These RNA effects are rarely covered by DNA-only safety screens.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: src_4f2097fc62 reports in mice that RNA SNV counts correlate positively with CBE expression across tissues. src_6117bfb6ea is metadata only (title), so its findings cannot be characterised beyond the title. The clinical consequence of transient RNA edits is not established in these abstracts.

findings.claim: Computational off-target prediction for base editors is only moderately reliable and is trained on cell-line reporter data. This limits its use as a stand-alone safety tool for therapeutic guide selection.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: src_1bf8d46372 reports Spearman correlations of 0.710 to 0.859 on a panel of endogenous loci. The models were trained on integrated reporter sites in human cells after five days of editing, and they target Cas9-dependent off-targets. The reported correlations show only moderate agreement, and the abstract does not say how well the models generalise to other cell types, editors or delivery modes. src_8f68bee9fc argues for experimental, base-editor-specific profiling because computational site selection introduces bias. The tool paper is an OpenAlex-indexed Nature Communications article, so I treat it as peer-reviewed.

findings.claim: Editing precision problems persist beyond off-targets. Mixed genotypes and undesired mutations within the intended editing window appear in microbial work, and reviews cite bystander editing, mosaicism, PAM limits and unresolved long-term safety.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The Clostridium result is from a bacterium that lacks effective DSB repair, so it is not directly transferable to human therapy. It also reported off-target SNPs and a 12 kb deletion removing UDG. The E. coli HiFi study (src_3e4582091d) is a proof-of-principle study that found a ~3-fold mutation-frequency increase with the BE. The review (src_39e3e10053) is a secondary source and appears to have no deep primary analysis. It states that the technology has not been used in therapeutic contexts, though that statement is at odds with the investigational-use item in src_8f68bee9fc.
findings.supporting_excerpt: most colonies exhibited mixed genotypes and most available protospacers led to undesired mutations within the targeted editing window.

findings.claim: Off-target risk profiles vary by species, chromatin context and deaminase behaviour, and profiling methods are not standardised. Safety results from one model or method may not transfer to humans or other methods.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The review (src_39e3e10053) is the direct source. Evidence in this set comes from mice, rice, tomato, bacteria and some human cells. This diversity itself makes cross-study comparison hard. The review is a lower-evidence secondary source whose own abstract mentions no new data.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Species-specific variability in off-target studies due to chromatin context and deaminase behavior raises the importance of standardized profiling pipelines.

hype_flags: 'Safe and highly effective' for tBE in β-hemoglobinopathies: the source is a conference abstract using ex vivo and patient-derived cells, with no clinical outcome data in the abstract.
'No detectable/undetectable off-target mutations': this is a statement about assay detection limits, and the abstracts do not give those limits. It is not a demonstrated zero.
'Base editing avoids double-strand breaks, so it is safer': the evidence here (CBE off-targets in mice, ABE8e-unique off-targets) shows the safety profile just shifts to different risks.

Single-patient customised ABE use cited in a CHANGE-seq-BE paper: this is a regulatory-use example, and the abstract gives no efficacy or safety outcome, so it should not be read as clinical validation.

finding.claim: S1 presents the CAR7 work as base editing having 'moved into human clinical testing' and implies a safety conclusion, but the abstract describes only three children, and the abstract text shown reports molecular remission in only the first patient. Three patients, with no follow-up reported in the available text, cannot establish safety or efficacy. The edited cells are also lentivirally transduced and have three simultaneous edits, so the result is not a clean test of base editing alone.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The cited abstract supports a very small, early-phase safety investigation. S1 and S7 build on the first-patient remission, which is an n=1 result, and the visible abstract is truncated before any later outcomes.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We investigated the safety of these edited cells in three children with relapsed leukemia.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S2 reports an 87% average conversion and a survival benefit in SMA mice, but the evidence is preclinical mouse data from a severe Δ7SMA model. The 87% figure is an average in mice and does not predict human tissue-level editing. S2 also omits the headline survival numbers (111 vs 17 days) and the point that the extension was seen with combined editor and nusinersen. The cited work itself speaks only of 'potential' for a one-time treatment.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract frames the result as potential. S7 turns 'permanent correction' into a shared design goal across therapeutic papers without noting that durability was not shown in humans, and that AAV9 delivery has its own immunogenicity and dosing questions not addressed in the abstract.
finding.supporting_excerpt: These findings demonstrate the potential of a one-time base editing treatment for SMA.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: The findings treat avoidance of double-strand breaks as a safety advantage (S5, S6) and never mention off-target risks. Independent evidence shows that base editors are not off-target-free. The CHANGE-seq-BE study found 98.8% of validated off-target sites were unique to ABE8e relative to Cas9 nuclease. A ~400-mouse, 15-month study found that BE3 produced de novo mutations, RNA SNVs and abnormal phenotypes. S6 relies on a 2026 self-published Zenodo book with no citations, which is promotional framing and not evidence of safety.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: S5's claim of improved 'product purity' and S6's 'without fracturing the genetic backbone' omit evidence that no DSB does not mean fewer off-target edits. The ABE8e comparison is an in vitro assay, so the clinical consequence is unproven. S6's source is a non-peer-reviewed book.
finding.supporting_excerpt: 98.8% of validated off-target sites were unique to ABE8e adenine base editors compared to Cas9 nuclease, suggesting substantially higher off-target activity of the former.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S3 labels as verified_fact that base editing 'can correct disease-causing mutations in cardiac tissue' and in organellar DNA. Both cited items (src_e6da2359ca and src_83eb4b0627) have no abstract in the evidence, only titles and metadata. The organellar paper is a review, not a demonstration of correction. The verified_fact label is therefore not supported by retrievable text, and mitochondrial editing is an inference (S8 itself says 'likely mitochondrial').
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Both records show 'no abstract available'. A title alone cannot verify the claimed correction, its efficiency or its safety. S3 should be downgraded to an interpretation or unverified claim.

finding.claim: S8 reads breadth across tissues and organisms as the technique being 'pushed across several boundaries'. The corpus is a small, selected set of papers with different maturity: a human trial in 3 patients, mouse studies, a plant book chapter and a title-only review. This variety shows topic coverage, not that base editing translates across tissues. It also ignores the known limits, namely bystander edits, mosaicism, PAM restrictions and species-variable off-target profiles, which were reported in the corpus.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Preclinical results in one species or tissue do not transfer directly, as src_39e3e10053 states. The Clostridium paper shows mixed genotypes and undesired mutations in the editing window, so breadth of application comes with precision caveats.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Species-specific variability in off-target studies due to chromatin context and deaminase behavior raises the importance of standardized profiling pipelines.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S9 forecasts a near-term shift to combining base editing with existing modalities as a bridge or adjunct. The cited papers do not support a trend. They contain one mouse co-administration experiment and a single patient who went on to transplant. Two instances are anecdotal. The CAR7 abstract also does not say that the transplant was planned as part of a combination strategy.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Extrapolating a direction from one mouse arm and one patient is weak. The forecast is correctly labelled low confidence, but it should state explicitly that there is no trend evidence.

finding.claim: S4 and S5 rest on a single plant-focused book chapter (src_5c4984e477) for general claims about human-relevant editing. The 'avoid DSBs and improve purity over Cas9' framing is a plant-science summary, and it presents prime editing as superior in scope without any comparison of efficiency or delivery. S5 treats the claimed improvements as established, although the abstract says 'aiming to improve' only in S5's own wording.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: A review chapter abstract reports claims without data. It supports what each technology can edit in principle, not relative performance. Sourcing from one chapter, with no primary comparative study, limits the conclusions.

limitations: Only 12 papers were provided. Five have no abstract (metadata only), so claims on them rest on titles alone.

Evidence is heavily weighted toward off-target effects, and the search did not return papers on delivery toxicity, immunogenicity, manufacturing cost, durability, or competing technologies (prime editing, nuclease editing, epigenetic editing). Absence of these topics is a coverage gap, not evidence that they are non-issues.
Several papers are in plants, bacteria or mice, so their relevance to human therapeutic risk is limited.
No arXiv preprints were included. All items were indexed through OpenAlex, but one is a conference abstract and one a review, so evidence quality is mixed.
Abstracts rarely report effect sizes, sample counts or detection limits, so confidence ratings stay low or medium.
No company or commercial product evidence was provided, so no company-specific risk could be assessed.

Only titles, metadata and abstracts were available. Several key papers (src_e6da2359ca, src_83eb4b0627, src_75ce59f10b, src_6117bfb6ea) have no abstract, so claims about them could not be verified or refuted.
Evidence for the contrarian points is a small retrieved set and is not a systematic review. Clinical outcomes beyond what the truncated NEJM abstract shows were not available.
Off-target assay results (CHANGE-seq-BE, mouse study) come from specific editors (ABE8e, BE3) and models, so they may not generalise to all base editors or to clinical products.
Many retrieved papers were irrelevant (NLP and image-editing preprints) and were ignored.

draft.summary: The evidence set shows base editing as a fast-growing research field that has reached very early human testing: research output is rising (code-computed counts 640 works in 2024 to 934 in 2025, with the partial 2026 year already at 1,219 versus 633 at the same point in 2025), and the science findings describe ex vivo edited CAR7 T cells in three children with relapsed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia [S1], AAV-delivered editing in a mouse model of spinal muscular atrophy [S2], cardiac and organellar work with title-only evidence [S3], and plant applications [S5]. Commercially, the field is dominated in the filings by Beam Therapeutics, whose 10-K itself states that base editing is not yet clinically validated for human therapeutic use and that its approaches may never lead to marketable products [M1][M2], with clinical-stage activity described only in press releases [M3] and with partnerships rather than disclosed customers [M4]. The most important uncertainty is safety: independent work reports de novo mutations and adverse phenotypes in a 15-month mouse study of a cytosine base editor [R1] and a distinct off-target footprint for a highly active adenine base editor [R2], while the risk challenges argue that the science findings overstate the clinical translation [C1][C2][C3][C4][C5]. Patent evidence is absent because the Patent agent did not run, and there are no social signals because the X agent did not run.
draft.plain_summary: Base editing is a way of rewriting a single letter of DNA without cutting the strand, and researchers are testing it as a treatment for inherited diseases, blood cancers and some plant traits. The science is moving quickly, but the only human evidence in this material is a handful of patients and the rest is animal or laboratory work, so it is far too early to say it works as a medicine. The main thing that could stop it is unintended changes to DNA or RNA elsewhere in the genome that safety tests may not yet reliably catch.

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: Near-term evidence is about clinical activity and announcements, not outcomes: Beam's press releases indicate BEAM-302 in a Phase 1/2 study for AATD and BEAM-304 dosing planned for early 2027 for PKU [M3], while Beam's own 10-K states base editing is not yet clinically validated and its approaches may never lead to marketable products [M2]. The only human base-editing report in the science findings is three children and does not, on the available text, establish safety or efficacy [S1][C1]. Timing risk is volatility rather than an extended price: Beam is 3.2% above its 50-day average but 31.0% below its 100-day high with 79.2% annualised volatility [T1][T2], and most names in the theme sit at or below their 50-day averages [T13].

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: What the evidence supports is that several programmes should read out, and that durability from a limited number of doses is the shared design goal [S7]. What it does not support is any assumption that mouse or cell results translate: the SMA work is a severe mouse model with an average 87% conversion and a survival benefit that also involved co-administered nusinersen [S2][C2], and 87% in mice does not predict human tissue-level editing [C2]. Delivery, dose and immunogenicity evidence is absent from this set.

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: The long-horizon question is whether permanent edits stay safe over years: the design goal is durable correction from limited dosing [S7], and the only long-duration in vivo safety data in the set is a ~400-mouse, 15-month study in which a cytosine base editor produced de novo mutations and adverse phenotypes [R1]. Nothing in the findings shows commercial-scale manufacturing, pricing, reimbursement or long-term human follow-up, so no long-horizon commercial conclusion is possible.

bull.label: ai_interpretation
bull.narrative: Base editing has crossed from concept into human testing and spans several tissue and organism settings [S1][S8], and multiple funded companies are running clinical-stage programmes with partnership validation from larger pharma [M1][M3][M4][M5]. If the durability-from-limited-dosing design goal holds [S7], the addressable set of monogenic diseases is large.

base.label: ai_interpretation
base.narrative: The realistic picture from this evidence is a field with strong research momentum, one very small human dataset and a set of preclinical programmes, where companies describe clinical activity in press releases while their own filings warn that base editing is not clinically validated [M2][M3]. Industrial structure is consolidating around a few platform owners plus partnerships and cross-licences [M4][M5], with an RNA-editing alternative positioning itself against DNA editing [M7][M8].

bear.label: ai_interpretation
bear.narrative: The bear case rests on unresolved safety and translation gaps: base editors are not off-target-free, with most validated off-target sites for one high-activity editor being unique to it relative to nuclease editing [R2], and a long-duration mouse study showing de novo mutations and adverse phenotypes [R1]. The clinical evidence is three patients with three simultaneous edits and lentiviral transduction, which cannot establish safety or efficacy [C1], preclinical mouse conversion rates do not predict human editing [C2], and the broader 'cross-tissue' reading of the corpus is topic coverage rather than demonstrated translation [C5].

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Read-outs or updates from the Phase 1/2 base-editing programmes described in filings, such as BEAM-302 in AATD and the planned BEAM-304 dosing in PKU [M3], would add clinical data where the current human evidence is three patients [S1][C1].

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Independent, standardised off-target profiling results — including methods that detect edits missed by DNA-only screens — would materially change how the safety question is judged [R3][R4][R7].

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Transition of the partnership and licence relationships described in filings into disclosed paying programmes would be a commercial signal beyond the current collaboration language [M4][M10].

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: Off-target DNA and RNA edits: base editors are not off-target-free [R2], RNA off-target SNVs scale with editor expression [R4], and 'no detectable off-targets' claims depend on assay sensitivity and bias [R3].

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: Within-window imprecision: bystander editing, mixed genotypes, mosaicism and PAM limitations are reported, with long-term safety unresolved [R6][R7].

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: Delivery and translation risk: the in vivo evidence is AAV delivery in a severe mouse model with an average conversion figure that does not predict human tissue-level editing [S2][C2].

themes.name: RNA base editing as an alternative modality to DNA base editing
technologies: Repeat-dosing RNA medicines as an alternative to permanent genomic edits

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: The evidence for this modality is early clinical and pipeline-stage: Wave Life Sciences' WVE-006, partnered with GSK, is in a Phase 1/2 study, and Korro Bio expects a new development candidate in 2026 [M7]. Wave positions its approach as avoiding irreversible collateral bystander edits and indels associated with DNA base editing [M8] — a competitive claim in a filing, not independent evidence. Timing risk here is the highest in the theme set: Korro is 26.9% above its 50-day average with 130.0% annualised volatility [T7][T8], while Wave is 44.6% down over three months [T11][T12].

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: The key open question the evidence raises is durability: DNA base editing is being pursued precisely for permanent correction from limited dosing [S7], whereas an RNA-level approach implies repeat administration. The findings contain no head-to-head efficacy, durability or dosing data between the modalities, and the safety-advantage claim comes from a competitor's own filing [M8], so no medium-term conclusion is supported.

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: There is no long-horizon evidence for this modality: the findings name programmes and a development-candidate expectation but no Phase 3 activity, approvals, manufacturing scale or reimbursement data [M7]. Any long-term view would be assumption, not evidence.

bull.label: ai_interpretation
bull.narrative: An RNA-level editing approach may sidestep the durability-versus-safety trade-off that dominates DNA base editing: Wave claims WVE-006 avoids irreversible collateral bystander edits and indels associated with DNA base editing [M8], at a time when independent work shows DNA base editors produce de novo mutations, adverse phenotypes in long mouse studies and distinct off-target footprints [R1][R2]. A large-pharma partnership with GSK and a named development candidate expectation provide external validation of the modality [M7].

base.label: ai_interpretation
base.narrative: RNA base editing appears in the evidence as a competitor modality referenced by other filers rather than as a demonstrated therapy: Wave's programme is in Phase 1/2 and Korro's candidate is still expected [M7]. Its claimed advantages come from the companies' own filings and are not corroborated here [M8], and the DNA editing programmes it competes with are themselves only in early trials [M2][M3].

bear.label: ai_interpretation
bear.narrative: The bear case is that the safety advantage is a marketing claim, not evidence: the assertion that RNA editing avoids bystander edits and indels is made in a competitor's own filing [M8], and the modality may need repeated dosing where DNA editing is designed for one-time permanent correction [S7]. Financials in the evidence are weak for the named smaller names — Wave shows fiscal 2025 revenue of 0.04B USD with revenue growth of -60.5% and R&D at 427.8% of revenue [K5] — and price behaviour is either sharply extended (Korro) or in a deep decline (Wave) [T7][T8][T11][T12], which is timing risk, not a signal in either direction.

catalysts.label: forecast

catalysts.label: forecast

risks.label: ai_interpretation

risks.label: ai_interpretation

themes.name: Base editing safety, off-target profiling and guide-selection tooling
technologies: Genome-wide off-target assays for base editors
RNA off-target detection for deaminase-based editors

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: The evidence shows active method development and active disagreement: base-editor-specific assays reveal off-target sites unique to a high-activity editor relative to Cas9 nuclease [R2], long-duration mouse work reports de novo mutations and adverse phenotypes [R1], and RNA off-target SNVs scale with editor expression [R4]. There is no commercial, revenue or customer evidence for safety tooling anywhere in this theme, so nothing supports a near-term commercial read.

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: Computational prediction for base editor off-targets is only moderately reliable and trained on cell-line reporter data, which limits its use as a stand-alone safety tool for therapeutic guide selection [R5]. Off-target profiles vary by species, chromatin context and deaminase behaviour, and profiling methods are not standardised [R7], so the medium-term question is whether standardisation happens — the findings do not show that it has.

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: No long-horizon evidence exists for this theme: the findings describe methods and their limitations, not products, customers, market size or regulation [R3][R5][R7]. Any long-term statement would be assumption.

bull.label: ai_interpretation
bull.narrative: If base editing therapies advance, the safety-screening layer becomes a gating requirement: off-target claims depend on assay sensitivity and bias [R3], RNA off-target effects are rarely covered by DNA-only screens [R4], and assay results do not transfer cleanly between species and contexts [R7]. Better methods therefore have a functional driver, and the field is already producing editor-specific assays and prediction tools [R2][R5].

base.label: ai_interpretation
base.narrative: The evidence describes a research and methodological capability with clear scientific demand but no demonstrated commercial structure: assays and predictors exist [R2][R5], their reliability is qualified [R3][R5], and no finding names a customer, product or revenue stream for safety tooling. Research activity of this kind is not commercial success.

bear.label: ai_interpretation
bear.narrative: The bear case for tooling as an investment theme is simply that the evidence stops at the laboratory: predictions are only moderately reliable and trained on reporter cell lines [R5], detection claims are method-dependent so absence of detected off-targets is not absence of off-targets [R3], and profiling is not standardised across species or chromatin contexts [R7]. Without any company, customer or commercial finding, this theme cannot be assessed as an investment at all on this evidence.

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Emergence of standardised, unbiased off-target profiling accepted across developers would change how safety data are interpreted and compared [R3][R7].

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Validation of computational off-target prediction on primary human cells or in vivo systems rather than cell-line reporter data would raise its usefulness for therapeutic guide selection [R5].

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: Detection-dependence: 'no detectable off-targets' claims are only as strong as the assay used, and absence of detection should not be read as absence of off-targets [R3].

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: RNA editing off-target effects are recurrent and are rarely covered by DNA-only safety screens [R4].

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: No commercial evidence: no finding in this theme names a product, customer or revenue for safety tooling, so any investment case would rest on assumption rather than evidence [R5][R7].

invalidation_conditions.label: forecast
invalidation_conditions.text: A demonstration that current guide-selection and screening practice already controls DNA and RNA off-target burden adequately would remove the functional driver for additional tooling [R3][R4].

invalidation_conditions.label: assumption
invalidation_conditions.text: Convergence on a single in-house screening method used by all developers would reduce the standalone value of third-party tooling, though no such convergence is evidenced [R7].

conflicting_evidence.label: ai_interpretation
conflicting_evidence.text: Several studies report no detected off-target effects while independent profiling finds editor-unique off-target sites and long-term adverse phenotypes in mice, so the findings conflict on how safe base editors can be shown to be [R2][R3][R1].
